explanations.answer: Strike them out of his hands
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. God tells Ezekiel, His prophet, what will happen to Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. He says, “Then I will strike the bow from your left hand and dash down the arrows from your right hand.” Gog shows up armed, and his weapons get knocked right out of his hands.

explanations.answer: Make them too heavy to lift
explanations.explanation: I see why that sounds fun, like a bow that weighs as much as a sack of flour. But God doesn't say the weapons get heavy. He says He will strike the bow from Gog's left hand and dash the arrows down from his right (Ezekiel 39:3). Gog is the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and Ezekiel is the prophet God is speaking through. The weapons get knocked away, not weighed down.

Burying does come up in this passage, but it isn't about the bow and arrows. God says He will strike the bow from Gog's left hand and dash the arrows down from his right. The burying comes later, and it is for Gog and his hordes (Ezekiel 39:11). The weapons get burned for fuel (Ezekiel 39:9), and the burial is for people.
Not quite, friend. God says, “On the mountains of Israel you will fall…” and He means more than Gog. His troops and the nations with him fall there too. Nobody gets away on this one.

Right. God doesn't single Gog out for falling while everybody else slips off. He says, “On the mountains of Israel you will fall…” and then names Gog's troops and the nations with him as falling too. That's the whole crowd, not one guy taking the hit for everybody.
That's it. God says Gog will fall in the open field, “…for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.” He gives no list of reasons. His word is the reason, and it's plenty.

I get the thought, but God never says that here. The reason He gives is short: “…for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.” Nothing in the verse mentions Israel's readiness. He points to His own word, and that's all the verse points to.

That's a natural guess, since battles usually come down to numbers. But the verse never counts anybody. God says, “…for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.” Gog falls because of what God has said, and the text leaves the headcount out of it.

Yes, that's the one. God says He will send fire on Magog and on the coastlands, “and they will know that I am the LORD.” That's what He wants them to know. And notice that He says it plainly, with no fancy words.

Close to the topic, but God doesn't say that. After the fire, He says they will know something about Himself: “…and they will know that I am the LORD.” The verse doesn't say anything about how strong Israel is. The focus stays on who He is.

That's not in this verse, friend. God says He will send fire on Magog and on those in the coastlands, “and they will know that I am the LORD.” He doesn't mention idols here. The lesson is about who He is.
That's right. God says, “Yes, it is coming, and it will surely happen, declares the Lord GOD.” Then He adds, “This is the day of which I have spoken.” He doesn't leave any maybe in it.

explanations.answer: It may happen if Israel repents
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd reach for that, but God doesn't attach a condition here. He says, “Yes, it is coming, and it will surely happen, declares the Lord GOD.” There's no if in that sentence. He makes it a sure thing.

explanations.answer: It depends on what Gog chooses
explanations.explanation: That sounds like Gog is steering, but look at what God says earlier. He tells Gog, “I will turn you around, drive you along, bring you up from the far north…” (Ezekiel 39:2). Then He says of the day, “Yes, it is coming, and it will surely happen, declares the Lord GOD.” God gives no "depends" about it.

Yes, friend. God says the people from Israel's cities will go out, kindle fires and burn the weapons. “For seven years they will use them for fuel.” Everything from bucklers to spears goes into the fire.

I know that picture from another place, swords into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4). But that's not what God says here. In this passage, the people kindle fires and burn the weapons, and God says they will use them for fuel (Ezekiel 39:9). The weapons go in the fire.
Nope, there's no stockpile here. God says the people will go out, kindle fires and burn the weapons. “For seven years they will use them for fuel.” Nothing gets saved for later.
Yes. God says, “They will loot those who looted them and plunder those who plundered them, declares the Lord GOD.” The ones who took from Israel get taken from. It's in the text just like that.

Not this time, friend. It's in the verse. God says, “They will loot those who looted them and plunder those who plundered them, declares the Lord GOD.” So True is the answer on this one, straight from Ezekiel 39:10.
That's the name. God says Gog and all his hordes will be buried in the Valley of the Travelers, “So it will be called the Valley of Hamon-gog.” The name comes straight from the burying.

Achor is a real valley, but it belongs to a different story. It shows up in Joshua 7:24-26, where Israel took Achan to that valley. In this passage, God says the valley where Gog and his hordes are buried will be called Hamon-gog (Ezekiel 39:11). Same Bible, different valley.

Hinnom is another real valley, down by Jerusalem. It shows up in Joshua 15:8 as part of a border line. But here, God names the burial valley for Gog and his hordes, and the name is Hamon-gog (Ezekiel 39:11).

That's the word. God says, “For seven months the house of Israel will be burying them in order to cleanse the land.” He uses the word again in verse 16: “And so they will cleanse the land.” It takes seven months, so nobody is rushing it.

Claiming sounds like a reasonable word, friend. But the text says they bury Gog's hordes “in order to cleanse the land” (Ezekiel 39:12). Cleansing is what the burying is for. Nobody's planting a flag.

I can see why that came to mind, like splitting up a pan of cookies. But God doesn't say anything about dividing the land here. He says the house of Israel buries the hordes for seven months “in order to cleanse the land.” Cleansing is the word.

Not quite. The bone does get buried, but not right where it lies. God says anyone who sees a human bone “will set up a pillar next to it, until the gravediggers have buried it in the Valley of Hamon-gog.” The passerby marks it, and the gravediggers handle the rest.

Yes, friend. Whoever spots a human bone doesn't dig anything. God says that person “will set up a pillar next to it, until the gravediggers have buried it in the Valley of Hamon-gog.” It's a marker for the gravediggers, so they can find it and bury it in the valley.

Yes. God tells Ezekiel, “Assemble and come together from all around to the sacrificial feast that I am preparing for you, a great feast on the mountains of Israel.” The birds and beasts are the ones being called. It's a big gathering, so I hope somebody brought a timer.

This one is straight from the verse, friend. God tells Ezekiel to call the birds and beasts: “Assemble and come together from all around to the sacrificial feast that I am preparing for you, a great feast on the mountains of Israel.” So True is the answer here. It's right there in Ezekiel 39:17.

That's the one. God says, “I will display My glory among the nations, and all the nations will see the judgment that I execute and the hand that I lay upon them.” What they see is what He does, and they see it with their own eyes.
Not what the verse says, friend. God says the nations will see “the judgment that I execute and the hand that I lay upon them.” Money doesn't come into it. What they see is His doing.

That's a different subject than what this verse says. God says, “I will display My glory among the nations, and all the nations will see the judgment that I execute and the hand that I lay upon them.” No temple gets mentioned in verse 21. The nations are watching what God does.

Yes. God says the nations will know “that the house of Israel went into exile for their iniquity, because they were unfaithful to Me.” That's the reason, and He states it Himself. It's a hard line, and He doesn't dress it up.

I see where you went, but that's not what God says. He says the nations will know “that the house of Israel went into exile for their iniquity, because they were unfaithful to Me.” The reason is about unfaithfulness. Nobody counts soldiers in this verse.

That sounds like a good plot twist, but it isn't in the text. God says Israel “went into exile for their iniquity, because they were unfaithful to Me.” Then He says He delivered them into the hands of their enemies (Ezekiel 39:23). Allies don't come up.
That's right. God says, “…because they were unfaithful to Me. So I hid My face from them…” He tells it plainly. It's a heavy part, and He doesn't pretend otherwise.

Not this time, friend. The verse says it directly: Israel “…were unfaithful to Me. So I hid My face from them…” So True is the answer. It's a heavy part of the passage, and it's right there in Ezekiel 39:23.

Yes, friend. After the "Therefore," God says, “Now I will restore Jacob from captivity and will have compassion on the whole house of Israel…” The story turns here, from exile toward bringing them back. It's a good turn.

explanations.answer: Give them the land of Magog
explanations.explanation: That's not what God says. He says, “Now I will restore Jacob from captivity and will have compassion on the whole house of Israel…” Magog is where He says He'll send fire (Ezekiel 39:6). Nobody gets handed it.

This passage never mentions a new army for Israel. God says, “Now I will restore Jacob from captivity and will have compassion on the whole house of Israel…” What He promises is a bringing back, with compassion. He doesn't promise a bigger battalion.

That's the word. God says, “They will forget their disgrace and all the treachery they committed against Me, when they dwell securely in their land, with no one to frighten them.” The disgrace stops weighing on them. It's a gentle promise.

I understand why that one pops up, but it's the opposite. God says, “They will forget their disgrace and all the treachery they committed against Me…” The word is forget, and it comes when they dwell securely in their land.

That one sounds like something that happens in a bad habit, friend. But the verse says something kinder. God says, “They will forget their disgrace and all the treachery they committed against Me…” No repeating, just forgetting, once they dwell securely in their land.

Yes. God says, “When I bring them back from the peoples and gather them out of the lands of their enemies, I will show My holiness in them in the sight of many nations.” Many nations get to see it. And God is the one who shows it.
Not in this verse, friend. God says He will gather them out of the lands of their enemies and “…show My holiness in them in the sight of many nations.” The word is holiness, not riches.

Anger is a natural guess, since this passage has some heavy parts. But in verse 27, God says, “I will show My holiness in them in the sight of many nations.” That's what many nations get to see when He gathers them. The word is holiness.

Not quite, friend. God says the opposite: He will regather them to their own land, “not leaving any of them behind after their exile among the nations.” Nobody gets missed. That's a promise with no loose ends.

Yes. God says He will regather them to their own land, “not leaving any of them behind after their exile among the nations.” He means everybody, and He doesn't miss a single one. It's the kind of gathering where no one gets left standing at the door.

That's the word. God says, “And I will no longer hide My face from them, for I will pour out My Spirit on the house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD.” The passage ends there, and it's a good place to land. Friend, you made it all the way through.

I see why that came up, since this passage has plenty of judgment in it. But the last verse turns, and God says, “I will no longer hide My face from them, for I will pour out My Spirit on the house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD.” What He pours out is His Spirit.

That's a thoughtful guess, but it isn't the word in the verse. God says, “And I will no longer hide My face from them, for I will pour out My Spirit on the house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD.” He pours out His Spirit. Nothing about law shows up in Ezekiel 39:29.
